intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the NEFL gene (162280) on chromosome 8p21.

checks.claim: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the NEFL gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the neurofilament light chain gene (NEFL) cause early onset severe Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports NEFL mutations causing CMT but does not say whether they are heterozygous or homozygous, and it does not use the name CMT1F. Homozygous mutation is not mentioned (abstract only).

paragraphs.text: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is a peripheral neuropathy caused by mutation in the neurofilament light chain gene (NEFL). Onset is early and the clinical course is often severe. Nerve conduction velocities are slowed, often in the demyelinating range. Both dominantly inherited forms, caused by heterozygous missense mutations, and recessively inherited forms, caused by homozygous nonsense mutations, have been reported.

checks.claim: CMT1F is a peripheral neuropathy caused by mutation in the neurofilament light chain gene NEFL.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the neurofilament light chain gene (NEFL) cause early onset severe Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports NEFL mutations causing CMT, a peripheral neuropathy. The CMT1F name is a nomenclature label.

checks.claim: CMT1F has an early onset.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients have an early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype.

checks.claim: The clinical course of CMT1F is often severe.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients have an early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype.

checks.claim: Nerve conduction velocities in CMT1F are slowed, often in the demyelinating range.
checks.evidence_quote: As predicted, the reduced axonal caliber results in markedly slowed nerve conduction velocities well into the “demyelinating range”.
checks.explanation: Conduction velocities in the demyelinating range are stated directly.

checks.evidence_quote: nonsense NEFL mutations probably cause a recessive phenotype, in contrast to missense mutations, which cause a dominant phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) proposed the term 'severe, early-onset axonal neuropathy' (SEOAN) for the disorder in their patients, who were homozygous for an NEFL nonsense mutation. They stated that under the OMIM designation for recessive axonal neuropathies, their patients should be called CMT2B5. They also emphasized that homozygous NEFL mutations should be considered when evaluating children with Dejerine-Sottas neuropathy.

paragraphs.text: Jordanova et al. (2003) screened 323 patients with CMT or related peripheral neuropathies and found NEFL mutations in some of them. Patients with NEFL mutations had an early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype. On electrophysiologic examination, nerve conduction velocities were moderately to severely slowed. Jordanova et al. (2003) also reported the first nerve biopsy from a CMT patient with a de novo NEFL missense mutation. It showed axonal pathology with axonal regeneration clusters and onion bulb formations.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) reported 4 affected children among the 5 children of first-cousin Palestinian parents. The affected children were 2 females and 2 males, aged 23, 17, 16, and 13 years at the time of the report. All 4 had hypotonia in infancy and early childhood, mildly delayed motor milestones, and slowly progressive atrophy and weakness of the distal muscles of the feet and hands. Bilateral pes cavus was described in all 4. The index patient (II-4) presented at age 2 years with toe walking. In 2 of the sibs the initial neuropathy symptom was a gait abnormality, and in the youngest it was delayed walking. All affected children had glove-and-stocking sensory impairment and absent ankle jerks. Patient II-1 also had moderate proximal leg weakness and a waddling gait, and her ambulation was walker-dependent. Patient II-4 had mild to moderate proximal arm and shoulder girdle weakness. Patient II-1 had learning difficulties, but the other affected children did not. Brain MRI was normal in 3 of the affected children (II-1, II-3, and II-4) and was not done in patient II-5.

paragraphs.text: In the sibs reported by Yum et al. (2009), motor nerve conduction velocities were severely slowed (12 to 25 m/s), even in early childhood; in patient II-5 slowing was documented from age 4 months. Motor amplitudes became progressively smaller with age. The sural, ulnar, median, and radial sensory responses were all absent, with 2 exceptions: an ulnar response in patient II-3 at age 4 years and a radial response in patient II-5 at age 10, both of low amplitude (4.5 and 17.0 microV, respectively). Visual evoked responses were prolonged in 3 of the 4 affected children, which the authors took to indicate subclinical CNS axonal involvement. A sural nerve biopsy from patient II-4 showed a reduced number of myelinated axons, with a density of 1300/mm compared to approximately 6000/mm in normal controls. Myelinated axons contained microtubules, but intermediate filaments were not present.

paragraphs.text: Both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance of CMT1F have been reported. Jordanova et al. (2003) found heterozygous NEFL mutations in patients with sporadic or dominantly inherited CMT, including a de novo missense mutation in one patient. Abe et al. (2009) found heterozygous missense mutations in 5 unrelated Japanese patients and a homozygous nonsense mutation in 1 patient. In the consanguineous Palestinian family reported by Yum et al. (2009), all 4 affected sibs were homozygous for a nonsense mutation, both parents were heterozygous, and the unaffected sib did not carry the mutation, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: In 4 sibs from a consanguineous Palestinian family with severe, early-onset neuropathy, Yum et al. (2009) identified a homozygous c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, predicted to result in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation, and the unaffected sib did not carry it. No mutations were found in other genes for demyelinating or recessive axonal CMT. The mutation had not been found in more than 11,000 individuals analyzed at a diagnostic laboratory. In SW-13 vim- cells, the E210X mutant NFL protein did not form filaments. It showed a diffuse, largely nuclear pattern and accumulated at low levels. Unlike the dominant Q333P mutant, it did not interfere with filament formation by wildtype NFL or with the vimentin network. The authors concluded that these results suggested a simple loss of function.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) noted that conduction velocities in their patients fell in the 'demyelinating' range, even though NEFL is not prominently expressed by myelinating Schwann cells. They concluded that the slowed conduction was likely explained by the absence of large myelinated axons, which lacked intermediate filaments and probably failed to develop their normal calibers.

paragraphs.text: In 4 affected sibs born to first-cousin Palestinian parents, Yum et al. (2009) identified a homozygous c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, predicted to result in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. The sibs had a severe, early-onset neuropathy with severely slowed motor nerve conduction velocities. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation, and the unaffected sib did not carry it. The mutation had not been found in more than 11,000 individuals analyzed at a diagnostic laboratory. In SW-13 vim- cells, the mutant protein did not form filaments and accumulated at low levels in a diffuse, largely nuclear pattern. It did not interfere with filament formation by wildtype NFL or with the vimentin network, which suggested a simple loss of function.
